steps.tx: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, historically termed **subacute thyroiditis** or de Quervain thyroiditis, typically follows an upper respiratory viral illness and presents with exquisite anterior neck pain and tenderness. Laboratory evaluation characteristically reveals a markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (**ESR**), exceeding 50 to 100 mm/hour, along with suppressed TSH and low 24-hour **radioiodine uptake** below 1% to 2% due to follicular disruption and iodine leakage.
steps.say: Subacute thyroiditis follows a viral upper respiratory illness, presenting with severe anterior cervical tenderness radiating to the jaw. Marked elevation of the erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 50 to 100 mm per hour is characteristic, while twenty-four-hour radioiodine uptake is profoundly suppressed due to follicular disruption.

steps.tx: The natural clinical course of subacute, silent, and **postpartum thyroiditis** follows a predictable triphasic evolution: an initial thyrotoxic phase lasting 2 to 6 weeks, followed by a transient hypothyroid phase lasting several months, culminating in euthyroid recovery. During the transient hypothyroid phase, symptomatic patients may require temporary replacement with **levothyroxine**, which is subsequently tapered after 6 to 12 months to verify whether permanent thyroid failure has supervened.
steps.say: Subacute, silent, and postpartum thyroiditis follow a classic triphasic pattern: initial thyrotoxicosis from preformed hormone leakage, followed by transient hypothyroidism, and eventual recovery. Symptomatic patients in the hypothyroid phase benefit from temporary levothyroxine, which is later tapered to verify endogenous gland recovery.

left.title: Thyrotoxic Phase
points: Follicular disruption and colloid leakage
Elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH
Profundly suppressed radioiodine uptake
Treated with NSAIDs or beta blockers

right.title: Hypothyroid Phase
points: Depletion of preformed glandular stores
Subnormal free T4 and elevated TSH
Transient clinical fatigue and cold intolerance
Temporary replacement with levothyroxine

steps.tx: Both **silent thyroiditis** and **postpartum thyroiditis** are painless autoimmune disorders occurring predominantly in women, characterized by circulating **TPO antibodies** in over 60% to 80% of cases. Postpartum thyroiditis typically develops within the first 12 months following parturition, particularly in women with high gestational anti-thyroperoxidase titres or type 1 diabetes. Like subacute thyroiditis, 24-hour radioiodine uptake is low, reflecting follicular injury rather than hyperfunctioning synthesis.
steps.say: Silent and postpartum thyroiditis are painless autoimmune disorders linked to positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. Postpartum thyroiditis develops within twelve months of delivery, especially in women with gestational autoimmunity. Both disorders show low radioiodine uptake, distinguishing them from postpartum Graves disease.

steps.tx: The rare entity **acute suppurative thyroiditis** represents a life-threatening bacterial infection of the thyroid parenchyma, typically presenting with high fever, leukocytosis, and severe localized unifocal tenderness. In pediatric populations and young adults, recurrent left-sided bacterial thyroiditis frequently originates from a persistent congenital fourth branchial arch remnant forming a **pyriform sinus** fistula. Definitive management requires broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics, percutaneous or surgical drainage, and endoscopic obliteration of the fistulous tract.
steps.say: Acute suppurative thyroiditis is an aggressive bacterial infection presenting with fever, leukocytosis, and exquisite unilateral thyroid tenderness. In children, recurrent left-sided thyroid abscesses are usually caused by a congenital pyriform sinus fistula. Management mandates intravenous antibiotics, abscess drainage, and fistulous tract resection.

steps.tx: The rare condition **Riedel thyroiditis** is characterized by extensive invasive fibroinflammatory proliferation that extends beyond the thyroid capsule into adjacent cervical strap muscles, trachea, and carotid sheath. It represents a local manifestation of systemic **IgG4**-related disease. Clinical palpation reveals a stony-hard, fixed, woody goitre mimicking advanced anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Fibrous entrapment of adjacent cervical structures frequently leads to hoarseness, stridor, and permanent surgical **hypoparathyroidism**.
steps.say: Riedel thyroiditis is a rare IgG4-related fibroinflammatory disorder where dense connective tissue extends beyond the thyroid capsule into adjacent strap muscles and trachea. The gland feels stony-hard and fixed on palpation, mimicking anaplastic cancer, and can produce stridor, recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, and hypoparathyroidism.

left.title: Riedel Thyroiditis
points: Part of systemic IgG4-related sclerosing disease
Dense collagenous fibrosis extending into neck
Stony-hard fixed goitre on palpation
Managed with systemic corticosteroids and tamoxifen

right.title: Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer
points: Highly aggressive undifferentiated malignancy
Rapidly growing neck mass in elderly patients
Marked cellular pleomorphism and p53 mutations
Poor prognosis requiring multimodal palliative care

steps.tx: Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is categorized into two distinct forms that require opposing therapeutic strategies. **Amiodarone** **type 1 thyrotoxicosis** arises from iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in patients with underlying nodular goitre, displaying preserved vascularity on colour Doppler, and responds to antithyroid thionamides. Conversely, amiodarone **type 2 thyrotoxicosis** represents a drug-induced destructive thyroiditis occurring in normal glands, characterized by absent Doppler flow, requiring oral corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone.
steps.say: Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis comprises two distinct entities. Type 1 is an iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in abnormal glands with preserved vascularity, managed with thionamides. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis in normal glands with absent Doppler flow, managed with oral prednisolone.

steps.tx: The transient thyrotoxic state designated **Hashitoxicosis** occurs during the early inflammatory destructive phase of **Hashimoto thyroiditis**. It arises from acute autoimmune follicular disruption and uninhibited release of preformed colloid thyroxine into the circulation. Differentiating Hashitoxicosis from Graves disease is critical: Hashitoxicosis demonstrates low or patchy 24-hour radioiodine uptake and high anti-TPO titres. Initiating prolonged antithyroid drug therapy with **methimazole** is contraindicated because spontaneous transition to primary hypothyroidism occurs within weeks.
steps.say: Hashitoxicosis is a transient hyperthyroid phase caused by early follicular breakdown in Hashimoto thyroiditis. Circulating thyroid hormones leak into the blood, but radioactive iodine uptake is low or variable. Methimazole is not indicated because the thyrotoxicosis is self-limiting and rapidly transitions into hypothyroidism.

left.title: Hashitoxicosis
points: Destructive release of preformed hormone
Low or patchy 24-hour radioiodine uptake
High anti-TPO with negative or low TRAb
Treated conservatively with propranolol only

right.title: Graves Disease
points: Autonomous de novo hormone hypersecretion
Diffuse homogeneous high radioiodine uptake
High TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb)
Treated definitively with methimazole or radioiodine

steps.tx: In the management of painful **subacute thyroiditis**, clinicians must not prescribe antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole or propylthiouracil. Because follicular hyperthyroidism results from mechanical disruption and leakage of preformed colloid stores rather than active de novo glandular synthesis, a **thionamide** or radioactive iodine is pharmacologically ineffective. Symptomatic control is achieved with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or prednisolone, alongside nonselective beta-adrenergic blockade with propranolol.
steps.say: Do not administer antithyroid thionamides or radioactive iodine in subacute thyroiditis. The gland is not synthesizing new hormone, but rather leaking preformed colloid into the circulation. Management relies on nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or corticosteroids for neck pain, and beta blockers for thyrotoxic palpitations.
